name: audit_deps
description:
Check declared dependencies against the OSV vulnerability database

Reads the lockfiles or SBOM under `path` (go.mod, JavaScript, Python, Rust, PHP and Ruby lockfiles, CycloneDX, SPDX) and asks osv.dev about every pinned dependency: which are named in an advisory, with its severity and the versions that fix it. It reads, it does not scan: whether your code reaches the vulnerable function is for osv-scanner, trivy or grype. Ecosystems OSV does not know are counted and named. `offline` inventories without asking osv.dev; `recursive` walks a monorepo.

Safety: read.

offline.description: inventory the dependencies without querying osv.dev

path.description: directory holding the lockfile or SBOM, or the file itself; a repository URL is read in memory, not over MCP

recursive.description: walk subdirectories too, for a monorepo with a manifest per package

timeout.description: query timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 5m)

name: audit_kube_eol
description:
Software past or near its end of life: the control plane, the kubelets, and every image's release

Grades the control plane, every node's kubelet and each running image's release against endoflife.date as `eol_check` does: past end of life fails, within `warn-within` warns, else passes with the date. Images are matched by name through the catalogue's aliases, the tag read as a release. An untracked image, floating tag or tagless digest is a check that could not run, and `detail` lists each. A `namespace` grades only its images and the control plane.

Also called: kubernetes, outdated, unsupported, upgrade, stale, components.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

namespace.description: audit one namespace instead of the whole cluster

warn-within.description: warn about a release whose end of life is within this long, such as 90d (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1d to 730d)

name: audit_kube_netpol
description:
Namespaces with no NetworkPolicy — unrestricted pod-to-pod traffic

Every non-system namespace checked for at least one NetworkPolicy. With none, the cluster's default applies: every pod in the namespace can reach every other pod, in either direction. Cites CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 2.0.1 5.3.2.

Narrowed to a namespace it checks that one, including a system namespace if you name it explicitly.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

namespace.description: audit one namespace instead of the whole cluster

name: audit_kube_podsecurity
description:
Pods running privileged, in a host namespace, or with root not excluded

Every pod cluster-wide against three Pod Security Standards controls: a privileged container (fail), hostNetwork, hostPID or hostIPC (fail), and no assertion of non-root (warn), meaning neither the pod nor any container sets runAsNonRoot or a non-zero runAsUser. Init and ephemeral containers count. The non-root check approximates the securityContext merge: a pod asserting it at pod level is not flagged, one relying on the image's own USER is. A `namespace` narrows which pods are read.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

namespace.description: audit one namespace instead of the whole cluster

name: audit_kube_quotas
description:
Namespaces with no ResourceQuota — unbounded resource consumption

Every non-system namespace checked for at least one ResourceQuota. CIS Kubernetes Benchmark has no numbered control for this, so it cites the NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance's "Resource policies". A `namespace` checks that one, a system namespace included when named.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

namespace.description: audit one namespace instead of the whole cluster

name: audit_kube_rbac
description:
Broad RBAC: cluster-admin bindings and wildcard rules

Every ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin and every Role or ClusterRole rule with a wildcard verb, resource or apiGroup. cluster-admin bound to system:authenticated or system:unauthenticated fails, the default system:masters binding is info, anything else warns. Cites CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 2.0.1 5.1.1 and 5.1.3. A `namespace` checks that namespace's Roles only: ClusterRoleBindings and ClusterRoles are not examined, and the result says so. RoleBindings are never read.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

namespace.description: audit one namespace instead of the whole cluster

name: audit_mail
description:
Audit a domain's email authentication: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS

Answers "can somebody send mail as this domain" from the records it publishes: SPF (and how close it is to the ten-lookup limit), DMARC policy and reporting, DKIM for the `selector` you give (selectors are not enumerated), MTA-STS and TLS-RPT (the TXT record only) and MX, a null MX included. Every finding cites an OWASP Top 10:2025 category and a MITRE CWE. `detail` adds a section per area and the references.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

selector.description: DKIM selector to check (the s= tag of a DKIM-Signature)

timeout.description: lookup timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 5m)

name: audit_web
description:
Audit a web host: TLS, certificate, headers, cookies, exposure

One HTTPS request to `host`, graded: TLS version and cipher, certificate validity and expiry, the security headers it should send (HSTS, CSP, framing, cross-origin isolation), CORS reflection, cookie flags and leaked version details. Every finding cites an OWASP Top 10:2025 category and a MITRE CWE. `detail` adds a section per area and the references. Only the response the host volunteers is inspected.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 5m)

name: audit_why
description:
Trace one dependency back to what pulled it in

Draws `package` at the root with everything that requires it beneath, up to the dependencies the project names itself, so you can tell whether it was asked for or pulled in, and by what. Reads the manifests `audit_deps` reads and resolves or fetches nothing. Where the file carries no graph (go.mod only marks a require direct or indirect) it says so and hands over the package manager's own command with the package filled in.

Safety: read.

package.description: the package to trace, as the lockfile spells it

path.description: directory holding the lockfile or SBOM, or the file itself; a repository URL is read in memory, not over MCP

recursive.description: walk subdirectories too, for a monorepo with a manifest per package

name: cert_chain
description:
Show the certificate chain presented by a host

Over MCP it reads a PEM or DER file under the server's roots and dials no host; `cert_expiry` checks a live host, with a grant.

Safety: read.

target.description: a PEM or DER file, or a host[:port] or https:// URL to connect to (over MCP, a file only)

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: cert_expiry
description:
Check certificate expiry for one or more hosts

Connects to each host in `targets` over TLS and reports when its certificate ends: time left, date and a status (ok, WARN within `warn-within`, EXPIRED, INVALID before it begins), with TLS 1.0 and 1.1 flagged. The chain the host sends is graded and the certificate that ends first sets the row, named when it is not the leaf. An unreachable host is its row's ERROR and stops nothing. Rows are most urgent first, each naming its host. A target is never a file here, and each host needs a grant.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

targets.description: hosts to check (host[:port], or an https:// URL)

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

warn-within.description: flag a certificate that ends within this long, such as 30d (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1d to 730d)

name: cert_inspect
description:
Show certificate details for a host or PEM file

Over MCP it reads a PEM or DER file under the server's roots and dials no host; `cert_expiry` checks a live host, with a grant.

Safety: read.

target.description: a PEM or DER file, or a host[:port] or https:// URL to connect to (over MCP, a file only)

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: cert_pem
description:
Print the certificate chain as PEM

The certificates as PEM, for a ConfigMap, a Dockerfile COPY or `update-ca-certificates`; `cert_chain` draws them to be read. `include` chooses which: chain (the default) is everything the host presented, leaf the end-entity certificate alone, issuers the chain without the leaf. A presented chain is what the host chose to send and may be incomplete: this reports what arrived and never fills the gap from a trust store. Over MCP it reads a PEM or DER file under the server's roots and dials no host; `cert_expiry` checks a live host, with a grant.

Safety: read.

target.description: a PEM or DER file, or a host[:port] or https:// URL to connect to (over MCP, a file only)

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: cert_tls
description:
Report the negotiated TLS version and cipher for a host

Over MCP this always refuses: a file has no handshake to report, and a host is not dialled by this tool. `net_probe` with `tls` reports a host's TLS version and cipher, with a grant.

Safety: read.

target.description: a PEM or DER file, or a host[:port] or https:// URL to connect to (over MCP, a file only)

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: codec_b64
description:
Base64 encode or decode a value

Decoding accepts standard, URL-safe and unpadded variants, and the line breaks and spaces wrapped base64 arrives with, without being told which dialect: the caller already has the encoded value, so being forgiving about which produced it costs nothing. Bytes that are not plain text come back as a hex dump, and text holding a control or invisible character comes back as its exact value beside the dump.

Safety: read.

url.description: use the URL-safe alphabet when encoding

name: codec_hex
description:
Hex encode or decode a value

Decoding accepts the spellings hex is copied in: a 0x prefix, and bytes separated by colons, spaces or dashes, the way openssl prints a fingerprint. Bytes that are not plain text are shown as a hex dump, beside the exact value when they are text holding a control or invisible character.

Safety: read.

name: codec_jwk
description:
Read a JSON Web Key or key set: type, size, thumbprint, and whether it is private

Takes one JWK or a whole key set (an issuer's jwks_uri answer) and says what each key is: type and size, whether its point is on its curve, kid, use and alg, and the RFC 7638 thumbprint a DPoP cnf.jkt or a pinned key is compared against. Names a key holding private material, which a published set never should, and two keys sharing a kid. An x5c chain is read and checked against the key beside it. Private members are never printed.

Safety: read.

name: codec_jwt
description:
Decode a JWT, JWS or JWE for inspection: headers, claims, dates

Decodes a signed token (JWS), an encrypted one (JWE) or the JSON form of either, and names what a strict parser would refuse. A JWE's content is not read. Unverified, and labeled so, unless `key` is given: a public key, certificate or issuer's key set, which you fetch, since this never fetches a URL. Then the signature is checked by the algorithm the key decides, never the token, and a mismatch is an error. An HMAC signature is checked only against a shared secret the operator keeps in a file.

Safety: read.

key.description: the public key, certificate or key set to verify the signature with

name: codec_url
description:
Escape a value for a URL, or unescape one

Query-component escaping by default (spaces become +), the form almost everyone means by "URL encode this" — the value for a query string or form body. `path` escapes a path segment instead, where a space is %20 and + is a literal plus: decoding a path as a query turns c++.txt into "c  .txt".

Safety: read.

path.description: escape or unescape a path segment rather than a query value

name: debug_ansi
description:
Break down the escape sequences and hidden characters in a string

Walks `input` as a terminal would and names what each printable run or escape sequence does: modes left set (hidden cursor, alternate screen, mouse reporting), terminal requests and OSC sequences, decoded. Also names characters that hide themselves (bidi overrides, zero-width, C1 controls, tag characters), decoded to what they invisibly carry, as a prompt injection hides in a sentence. An escape written out as text (\033, \x1b, \e, ^[) is read as the character, and said to be.

Safety: read.

name: eol_check
description:
Whether a product, or one of its release cycles, is still supported

Looks up `product` on endoflife.date and grades every release cycle by how close it is to its end-of-life date. Name one `cycle` (or the version running, 16.2, for its cycle, 16) or a range (13..16, 15.., ..16) to see just those; leave it out to see every supported cycle and the latest one that has ended, or pass `all`. Aliases work: "postgres" and "postgresql" name the same product.

Safety: read.

all.description: list every cycle, including those long ended, when none is named

cycle.description: one release cycle — 15, bookworm, 22.04 — or a version in one, 16.2 — or a range of them: 13..16, 15.., ..16; every cycle when omitted

product.description: product name or alias — see https://endoflife.date for the catalogue

warn-within.description: flag a cycle whose end of life is within this long, such as 90d (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1d to 730d)

name: eol_products
description:
Search the endoflife.date catalogue: names, aliases and categories

Lists the products endoflife.date tracks, with the aliases `eol_check` and `eol_watch` accept for each. A term narrows the list to products whose name, label or alias contains it. Without one the first products are listed and the total says how many there are; `limit` shows more.

Safety: read.

category.description: only this category — database, os, framework, lang, …

term.description: part of a name, label or alias — postgres, kube, ubuntu

name: eol_watch
description:
Grade every product and cycle on a configured watchlist at once

Runs `eol_check` over a list of products, each optionally pinned to one release cycle or a range of them as product@cycle — postgresql@15, postgresql@13..16, nodejs, debian@bookworm. Write the list once as `plugins: eol: watch.products:` in your config or a profile and it is what this grades from then on. A product the API does not know, or a cycle the product does not have, is one row saying so; the rest of the list is still graded.

Safety: read.

products.description: product or product@cycle, repeatable — usually from `plugins: eol: watch.products:` in your config

warn-within.description: flag a cycle whose end of life is within this long, such as 90d (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1d to 730d)

name: fs_hash
description:
Checksum a file, and compare it against an expected value

Hashes the file at `path` and, given `expect`, says whether it matches. A file that is not the one described is an error, and a checksum that cannot be this algorithm's, by its length, is refused rather than reported as a mismatch. The comparison is case-insensitive and tolerates a "sha256:" prefix and surrounding whitespace. It is not a signature check: it says a file is the one somebody described, not who described it.

Safety: read.

name: fs_tree
description:
Show a directory as a tree, with sizes

The shape of a directory, a few levels at a time, with each entry's size beside it, directories first and then by name. A truncated branch says how many entries it hides, so the tree never claims a directory is smaller than it is. `detail` adds what the walk covered and everything it left out (depth, per-directory limit, hidden entries, mount points, unreadable directories) in one place. A name holding an escape or a newline is shown quoted, never cleaned into another name.

Safety: read.

name: fs_usage
description:
Show what is using space under a path, biggest first

Totals every entry under `path` and ranks them. Directories are summed recursively; the share column is of the scanned total, not of the disk. A size is the disk a file takes, as du counts it (a sparse file by what is written, a hard-linked file once); `apparent` counts lengths instead. `detail` adds the ranking, the largest files beneath it and what was skipped. Follows no symlinks and crosses no filesystem boundary. A name holding an escape or a newline is shown quoted, never cleaned into another name.

Also called: folder, directory.

Safety: read.

apparent.description: count each file by its length rather than the disk it takes

depth.description: how deep to descend when totalling (0 = no limit)

name: gen_overview
description:
A sampler of the shapes worth generating, ready to use

Generates one of each common shape side by side — passwords, encryption key material, URL-safe and TOTP tokens, UUIDs — labelled with what it is for, the entropy it actually carries and the call that reproduces it, so picking the right shape does not require remembering the inputs first. With `detail`: every preset, plus why a "32-character key" is not a 32-byte one. Every value is real and freshly generated; nothing is an example.

Safety: read.

name: gen_password
description:
Generate a cryptographically random password

Characters are drawn uniformly, with no modulo bias. Reports entropy in bits: length x log2(alphabet size).

Safety: read.

name: gen_token
description:
Generate random bytes, formatted as hex/base64/base32

crypto/rand bytes, formatted by `encoding`. base32 at the right length is already a TOTP secret (RFC 4648/6238) — there is no separate gen.totp.

Also called: api, secret, bearer, key, create.

Safety: read.

name: gen_uuid
description:
Generate a UUID: v4 random (default) or v7 time-ordered

v1/v3/v5/v6 are deliberately not offered: v1 leaks the generating machine's MAC address and a timestamp, v3/v5 hash a namespace+name instead of generating anything (a different operation), and v6 is superseded by v7 for the same time-ordering goal, per RFC 9562's own recommendation.

Safety: read.

name: git_blame
description:
Who last touched each line of a file, and when

One row per line: who last changed it, when, and the commit. `from` and `limit` show a window of the lines, and the total is the file's length. Refuses a version of the file over 16 MiB, or a history over 64 MiB. It spends at most two seconds on history: a line not traced by then carries the commit it had reached, marked ^ as git marks a boundary, meaning the line is at least that old.

Safety: read.

file.description: the file to blame, relative to the working directory (the repository's root if it has no checkout)

from.description: the first line to show, counting from 1

limit.description: how many lines to show from there; 0 shows the rest of the file

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_branches
description:
Local branches, what each tracks, and which one is checked out

Every local branch, alphabetically, with the checked-out one marked, the remote branch it tracks and how far the two have drifted as of the last fetch; nothing here touches the network. `gone` in Status means the tracked remote branch no longer exists, the usual sign a merged branch can go. `all` adds remote-tracking branches as `remotes/<remote>/<name>`. A detached HEAD is its own row, and a branch checked out in another worktree is marked `worktree`. Tracking is read as `git_remotes` reads a remote.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_config
description:
Effective config across system, global and local scope

Every key set in system, global, local or worktree config, one row per file it is set in with its scope, before any overrides another (worktree over local over global over system, the command scope over all). Includes are followed as git follows them; one that cannot be decided is not read, and a warning says so. Over MCP only the repository's own config, local and worktree, is returned, and an include of a file outside the server's roots is named in a warning and never opened. Credentials are masked.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_diff
description:
Line-level changes — uncommitted, or one commit against its parent

Unified diff text. With no `commit`, every uncommitted change, staged and unstaged, against HEAD. `commit` diffs that commit against its parent (the root against the empty tree, a merge against its first parent); two arbitrary commits are not compared. Limits: 16 MiB per file, 64 MiB and 10000 files in all, two seconds (past which it is refused as git.status.timeout); lines after the patch name each file left out or diffed coarsely. Over MCP a working-tree link is diffed only where it names a place under the roots.

Safety: read.

commit.description: diff this commit against its own parent, instead of the working tree against HEAD

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_hooks
description:
What's in the hooks directory, and which of it git would actually run

The hooks directory (core.hooksPath, else the repository's own) and which entries git would run, judged as git judges them: named exactly (a `.sample` suffix never runs) and executable, a symbolic link by what it leads to. Anything else with a hook's name, a directory or a named pipe, is one git tries to run and cannot, failing the command it guards, and is listed as fails. Over MCP a link leading outside the roots is not followed and is listed active, as git may run what it leads to.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_log
description:
Recent commit history

The most recent commits reaching HEAD, newest first — hash, author, date and the message's own first line, each a table row rather than text to parse. `file` narrows it to commits that touched one path — a file, or anything beneath a directory — the structured equivalent of `git log -- <path>`.

Safety: read.

file.description: commits touching this file or directory, relative to the working directory (the repository's root if it has no checkout)

limit.description: how many of the most recent commits to show

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_overview
description:
Branch, working-tree state and the latest commit, at a glance

A verdict (warn when a merge or rebase is half done, paths are unmerged or the upstream is gone), the branch checked out (or a detached HEAD), what it tracks as of the last fetch, with that fetch's age once it is a day old, whether the tree is clean, the stash and the latest commit. `detail` expands into the status, log and branches views their own tools return. The tree is read as `git_status` reads it, and past two seconds the overview is refused as git.status.timeout.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_remotes
description:
Where this repository fetches from and pushes to

Each remote with its URL, the config file that sets it and how many of its branches this repository knows from the last fetch (0 for a remote never fetched). A remote with a pushurl is two rows, and Use says which does what: git fetches from the first url and pushes to every pushurl where set, else every url. Read from every config file git reads, a url.<base>.insteadOf rewrite included; over MCP only the repository's own config, as `git_config` shows it there. Credentials in a URL are masked.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: git_status
description:
What has changed in the working tree, staged and unstaged

One row per path with a staged change, an unstaged change, or neither yet. A path a merge stopped on is listed as git lists it (UU, AA, UD, DU); a staged move with unchanged content is one `R` row, `old -> new` in Path. A submodule at another commit or with changes inside is modified. Ignore files apply, up to 1 MiB and 10000 patterns; a larger one, or a .gitignore that is a symbolic link, is skipped with a warning. Past two seconds it is refused as git.status.timeout, never answered with a cleaner tree.

Safety: read.

path.description: repository path, or a subdirectory of one; a remote URL is cloned in memory, not over MCP

name: gitignore_list
description:
List the templates github/gitignore offers

The templates in the github/gitignore repository, with the name `gitignore_show` takes for each: main ones (languages, frameworks, tools), global ones (operating systems, editors) and community ones. A `term` narrows to templates whose name contains it, or to one kind when it is main, global or community. Without one the first templates are listed and the total says how many there are; `limit` shows more.

Also called: ignore, template, generate.

Safety: read.

kind.description: only this kind: main (languages and tools), global (systems and editors), community

term.description: part of a template's name, or a kind (main, global, community) to list that kind: go, node, mac, global

name: gitignore_show
description:
Print github/gitignore templates as one .gitignore file

Prints the named github/gitignore templates as one .gitignore file, each file's text under its own ### name ### line. `templates` takes names as gitignore_list shows them, in any case, or a qualified name such as Global/macOS when a bare name could mean two.

Also called: ignore, template, generate.

Safety: read.

templates.description: template names as `gitignore_list` shows them: Go, Node, macOS; or a qualified name, Global/macOS, when a name could mean two

name: http_delete
description:
DELETE a URL

Also called: api, endpoint, request.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 10m)

name: http_get
description:
GET a URL and show status, timing and body

Also called: api, endpoint, request, fetch, curl, download.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 10m)

name: http_head
description:
HEAD a URL and show status, timing, type and declared size

Also called: api, endpoint, request.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 10m)

name: http_post
description:
POST to a URL with an optional body

Also called: api, endpoint, request, submit.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

data.description: request body, sent as given; a JSON object or array goes out as application/json unless a Content-Type header says otherwise

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 10m)

name: http_put
description:
PUT to a URL with an optional body

Also called: api, endpoint, request.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

data.description: request body, sent as given; a JSON object or array goes out as application/json unless a Content-Type header says otherwise

timeout.description: request timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 10m)

name: http_status
description:
What an HTTP status code means, and where it is defined

A code prints its card; a class (`4xx`, `500-599`) or nothing prints the table. Offline: the text is the standard's, and every code net/http knows is here. It looks at no URL: `http_head` reports the status a live one returns.

Safety: read.

code.description: a code (404), a class (4xx) or a range (500-599); every code when omitted

name: keys_list
description:
List the SSH private keys in ~/.ssh, how protected each is, and whether it can be backed up

Keys are found by their PEM preamble, not an id_* name, so a key under any name is listed. Only public data is read: the .pub sibling for type, fingerprint and comment, and whether the private key is passphrase-protected, checked without a passphrase. Nothing is decrypted. Backup-eligible means ed25519, the one type with a single seed to encode as words. An Exposed column appears only when another account on this machine can read a key.

Safety: read.

name: kv_env
description:
Print stored values as shell exports

Output for a shell to evaluate, which loads secrets into its session without ever writing them to a file. Key names become environment names (db-password → DB_PASSWORD). A `format` of dotenv writes .env syntax instead. Same grant requirement as `kv_get`: this reveals values. Naming no key means every key, which is a wider ask and needs a grant for `kv_env` itself rather than one per key.

Safety: write.

Returns the stored value itself, not a masked copy, and it becomes part of your context.

Requires a grant.

prefix.description: prepend this to every variable name, e.g. APP_

name: kv_get
description:
Reveal a stored value

Classified as a write, because revealing a secret is the sensitive act: an agent needs a grant naming the key it may read, issued by a person. A grant authorizes revealing a value, not choosing where on this machine it gets written, so the value comes back in the response.

Also called: secret, password, read, retrieve, credential, decrypt, store.

Safety: write.

Returns the stored value itself, not a masked copy, and it becomes part of your context.

Requires a grant.

name: kv_history
description:
What a key held before, and when each value was replaced

Every write over an existing key keeps what it replaced — the last 5 values, inside the same encrypted store — and `kv_rm` keeps the whole entry aside rather than destroying it. This lists that past: kind, size, description, when each value was set and when it was replaced. Never the values themselves, which is what keeps it a Read; `kv_restore` brings one back.

Safety: read.

name: kv_init
description:
Set up how the store is encrypted

Done once. `generate` makes a dedicated age key for this store and uses it: no passphrase to type, and unlike an SSH login key, one whose loss costs this store and nothing else. A passphrase store needs no init, which is what the store is by default. Locking it to a key that already exists, or adding readers, is the operator's to do.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

generate.description: create a dedicated age key for this store and lock it to that

name: kv_list
description:
List stored keys (names and metadata only, never values)

Key names, kind, size, description, when it changed and, once a value has been replaced, how many earlier values `kv_history` keeps. Never a value or a preview. `folder` is one folder of the tree `kv_tree` draws (`db/` for `db/password`); `match` is a case-insensitive substring of the name or the description, so `aws` finds a key whose description alone says AWS. `detail` adds the source filename of anything stored from disk.

Safety: read.

folder.description: only the keys in this folder, e.g. db/

match.description: only keys whose name or description contains this (case-insensitive)

removed.description: list what `kv_rm` set aside instead — restorable until purged

name: kv_overview
description:
What the secret store holds, by count and kind, and what can open it

How many keys and folders of each kind, the bytes of values, the age of the newest and oldest, and what is kept beside the live keys: earlier values (`kv_history`) and removed keys (`kv_restore`). Then where the store is, when it last changed, how it is locked and whether this environment can open it. Never a value. It never asks for what opens the store: with no key at hand it says so and answers the rest, and `kv_status` is cheaper. `detail` adds the biggest top-level folders and who can open a store locked to keys.

Also called: secrets, stored, inventory, contents, counts, locked, passwords, credentials, deleted.

Safety: read.

name: kv_recipients
description:
List the public keys that can decrypt the store

Answers "who can read this?" without unlocking anything — recipients are public keys, so the list is plaintext by design. An empty list means the store is passphrase-encrypted.

Safety: read.

name: kv_rekey
description:
Change which keys can open the store

Decrypts the store and writes it back under a new set of readers, the one operation that changes who can read what is stored. Adding is the default: `generate` makes a dedicated age key and keeps the existing readers; `only` makes the set exclusive, and with `generate` swaps one lock for the other. A store that cannot be opened, and a change that locks out every key the operator holds, are refused. Old copies and backups stay readable by the old keys.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

generate.description: create a dedicated age key for this store and add it

only.description: lock it to exactly these keys, dropping every other reader

name: kv_rename
description:
Rename a key, keeping its value and its history

Moves the entry to `new-name` inside the store with its value, description, kind, source, history and timestamps; the value is never decrypted outside memory, so this is the rename that reveals nothing. A name already taken is refused, not overwritten (that is `kv_rm`'s question). A grant must cover both `key` and `new-name`; a folder grant covers a move inside the folder.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

name: kv_restore
description:
Bring back a removed key, or an earlier value of one

With no `revision`, a key `kv_rm` removed comes back exactly as it was, history included. With one, the key's current value is replaced by that earlier one — the number `kv_history` lists, 1 being the most recent — and the value being replaced joins the history in turn, so a restore is itself undoable.

A removed key whose name has since been reused is refused rather than merged: rename the live one first, or purge the removed one.

Also called: deleted.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

revision.description: an earlier value to restore, as `kv_history` numbers them; omit to restore a removed key

name: kv_rm
description:
Remove a stored key, keeping it restorable until purged

The key leaves the listing and every read, but the entry is kept aside whole, history included, where `kv_list` shows it with `removed` and `kv_restore` brings it back. `purge` has no undo: the entry and everything it held are destroyed, and a key removed earlier is finished off too. Removing the last entry leaves an empty store locked to the same keys. `kv_rename` moves an entry without removing it.

Also called: delete, deleted.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

purge.description: destroy it, history included — no restore

name: kv_set
description:
Set (or overwrite) a stored value

Stores `value` under `key`. A call with no `value` is refused unless `description` or `kind` relabel an entry that exists, which leaves the secret and both timestamps alone. The kind (certificate, private key, json, file, string) is detected from the content unless `kind` says otherwise. Overwriting keeps the old value among the last 5 listed by `kv_history` and brought back by `kv_restore` with a `revision`. Needs a per-key grant; who can read the store is `kv_rekey`'s.

Also called: secret, password, save, write, credential, encrypt.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

description.description: what this is for — shown by `kv_list`

kind.description: override the kind detected from the content

name: kv_show
description:
Show everything about one entry except its value

The detail page for a stored key: what kind of thing it is, what it is for, how big it is, where it came from and when it changed. Deliberately not the value — that is `kv_get`, a write for exactly that reason. This stays Read because everything on it is metadata.

Safety: read.

name: kv_status
description:
Where the store is and what can open it

Everything about the store that can be known without unlocking it: whether it exists, how big it is, when it last changed, whether it is locked with a passphrase or to keys, and whether a key is available in this environment. It reads the file and never decrypts it, so it answers whatever state the store is in; `kv_overview` is the page that also counts what is inside, and carries these lines.

Safety: read.

name: kv_tree
description:
The store as a tree of the folders its keys share

Keys named with slashes — `staging/db/password`, `prod/deploy-key` — are drawn as the folders they share, each leaf labelled with its kind. Names only, never values, the same line `kv_list` draws. A grant for `kv_get` scoped to staging/ is how one of those folders becomes a grant's scope, so this is also the map of what such a grant covers.

Safety: read.

folder.description: only the keys in this folder, e.g. db/

name: net_dns
description:
Resolve DNS records for a name, or a name for an address

A `type` of auto (the default) asks the question you usually mean: A, AAAA and CNAME for a name, PTR for an address. The system resolver answers unless the operator has set another. With `detail`: the query, the resolver that answered, and how long it took.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

name.description: name or IP address to resolve

timeout.description: query timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

type.description: which record type to ask for

name: net_hosts_add
description:
Point a hostname at an address in the hosts file

A name resolves to one address, so this takes the name away from any other active entry rather than leaving two that race. Everything else in the file (comments, ordering, spacing) survives untouched, and the previous version is saved before the write. Destructive rather than write: it rewrites a root-owned file that governs name resolution for every process on the machine, and a wrong entry silently reroutes traffic instead of failing.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

name: net_hosts_list
description:
List hosts-file entries, including disabled ones

One row per hostname, since a hostname is what you look up, disable and remove. Entries commented out by `net_hosts_toggle` are shown as disabled rather than hidden as comments.

Safety: read.

file.description: operate on this file instead of the system one (a container's, a chroot's)

name: net_hosts_rm
description:
Remove hostnames from the hosts file

Removes the names, and the line only if nothing is left on it. `net_hosts_toggle` parks an entry instead, which is usually what you want.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

name: net_hosts_toggle
description:
Enable or disable a hosts-file entry without deleting it

A disabled entry stays in the file, commented, and comes back with the same command. Same blast radius as add, same classification.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

name: net_listen
description:
What this machine is listening on, and which process owns it

Every TCP and UDP socket open here, with its bound address, how far that reaches (loopback, one address, or all interfaces) and the process behind it. Two limits. UDP has no listening state, so a socket with a port and no peer shows whether it is a server or a resolver with a query in flight. And the answer is only as complete as the caller's privileges: Linux cannot name the process behind a socket it may not look into, so Process is empty; macOS reads through lsof, so the row is absent entirely.

Safety: read.

port.description: only this port — the "who has 8080" question

proto.description: only this protocol (tcp covers tcp6, udp covers udp6)

name: net_overview
description:
Local network overview: default route, traffic, DNS, hosts file, addresses

Local network state, read from this host alone. `status` is ok, or fail for no default route or no resolver; then `route` (gateway and interface), `traffic` (rx and tx per second over 500ms), `dns` (first resolver, how many fall back), `hosts` (names the hosts file adds, how many are parked), `ip` (IPv4 addresses) and `proxy` when set, credentials masked. A line that cannot be read says so; `numbers` has the figures. `detail` adds every interface, IPv6 addresses, every resolver and the hosts file.

Safety: read.

name: net_ping
description:
Ping a host and report latency statistics

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

graph.description: plot per-probe latency instead of summary stats

timeout.description: overall timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 5m)

name: net_port
description:
TCP connect-scan ports on a host

Which ports answer, not what they say — `net_probe` shows the banner for one; this maps many at once. Needs a grant for the same reason: the host is the caller's choice.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

ports.description: ports and ranges, comma-separated: 22,80,8000-8010 (up to 4096 at a time)

timeout.description: timeout per port (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 1m)

name: net_probe
description:
Open a TCP connection and report what answers

Proves the port accepts a connection, times the handshake, and shows the banner the service volunteers. `tls` completes a TLS handshake first and reports the negotiated version and cipher. It sends nothing and only waits for the banner; to speak first — the protocols that expect the client to open — use `net_send`, which is a write. Both need a grant: the destination is the caller's choice either way, and whatever it says back is read as tool output.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

tls.description: complete a TLS handshake after connecting, in whatever protocol the host speaks, TLS 1.0 on

wait.description: how long to wait for the service to say something (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: net_resolver_list
description:
Show the system resolver, and who controls it

resolv.conf is the file people most often edit to no effect: on most modern systems it is generated and replaced. This leads with who owns it, because that decides whether anything else in it is worth changing.

Also called: dns, nameserver, nameservers, servers, resolv.

Safety: read.

file.description: operate on this file instead of the system one (a container's, a chroot's)

name: net_resolver_set
description:
Set the system nameservers

Replaces the nameserver lines, leaving search domains, options and comments where they are, after saving the previous version. Refuses when the file is generated by something else — silently editing a generated file is worse than refusing, since the change works and then vanishes with nothing to point at. `force` overrides that, with the warning repeated in the result.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

force.description: write even when the file is machine-generated

name: net_send
description:
Send bytes to a TCP port and report what comes back

Opens a TCP connection, writes `data` and shows the reply: how you poke a protocol where the client speaks first (SMTP, Redis, HTTP/1.0). \r\n and \n in `data` are interpreted; `tls` speaks it over TLS, to a host whose certificate this machine trusts for the name you call it by. What arrives is executed by whatever is listening (FLUSHALL empties a Redis), so it is destructive. `net_probe` is the read-only half (connect, handshake, listen) and needs a grant too, since the destination is the caller's choice either way.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

timeout.description: connect timeout (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

tls.description: complete a TLS handshake before sending, TLS 1.2 or newer, with a host whose certificate checks out for its name

wait.description: how long to wait for a reply (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 2m)

name: net_trace
description:
Trace the route to a host, hop by hop

ICMP echo probes with a rising TTL: each hop that expires one reports itself. Answers the question ping cannot — not just "is it reachable" but "where does it stop". Silent hops show as *; that is a router declining to reply, not necessarily a fault.

Safety: read.

Requires a grant.

resolve.description: resolve hop addresses back to names

timeout.description: timeout per probe (with its unit, e.g. 30s, 5m; from 1s to 1m)

name: note_add
description:
Add a note

A title is enough. `todo` (or a due date, which implies it) makes it something to do; a parent makes it part of something bigger; markdown in the body is rendered on human surfaces.

Also called: remember, reminder, todo, task, jot, later.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

due.description: due date: today, tomorrow, a weekday, +3d, 2w, next-week, 10-20 or yyyy-mm-dd

parent.description: make this a sub-note of the given note id

todo.description: make it a to-do: something to check off

name: note_done
description:
Check notes off

Done for a task, filed for a note: either way it leaves the default list and stays findable through `note_list`'s `all`, and in `note_search`. Several ids check off several notes in one call, all or none: an id that is not a note refuses the call before anything changes. A plain note is made a to-do and checked off in the same call, since asking to be done with it says what it is.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

name: note_edit
description:
Edit a note's title, body, tags, due date or parent

Empty fields keep their current value, and `clear` empties the ones it names: the body, the tags or the due date. A `tag` of - also clears all tags, and a `due` of none the due date.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

body.description: new body, markdown supported (empty keeps the current one)

clear.description: fields to empty: body, tag (every tag), due

due.description: due date: today, tomorrow, a weekday, +3d, 2w, next-week, 10-20 or yyyy-mm-dd

parent.description: move it under this note id (0 makes it top-level)

title.description: new title (empty keeps the current one)

name: note_list
description:
List notes

Open notes, the ones with a due date first — soonest on top — then the rest in the order they were written. Checked-off notes are hidden unless `all`. Shows top-level notes by default; `parent` lists one note's sub-notes. With `detail`: adds creation date and a body preview.

Also called: todo, tasks.

Safety: read.

parent.description: list sub-notes of this note id instead of top-level notes

tag.description: only notes with any of these tags

name: note_reopen
description:
Reopen checked notes

The undo for `note_done`, for one id or several. Re-opening an already-open note is a no-op, not an error.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

name: note_rm
description:
Remove notes permanently

Sub-notes are re-parented to the removed note's parent, never deleted silently. Several ids remove several notes in one call, all or none, each one a record a grant or a consent has to cover.

Safety: destructive.

Requires a grant.

name: note_search
description:
Search notes by title, body or tag

Searches every note regardless of parent/child, done or open.

Also called: find, todo, lookup.

Safety: read.

name: note_show
description:
Show one note: metadata, content, sub-notes, references

A composed page rather than one blob: structured metadata (status, due, tags, parent, progress) stays separate from the markdown content, so both stay readable and machine callers can read a due date without parsing prose. Sub-notes and cross-references ("#12" in a body, resolved both ways) follow.

Safety: read.

name: note_tags
description:
List tags in use and how many notes carry each

Safety: read.

name: note_toggle
description:
Turn a note into a to-do, or a to-do back into a note

The switch between the two kinds of thing in the notebook. A note becomes an open to-do; a to-do becomes a note and forgets whether it was done, which is the point — a note has nothing to be done about.

Also called: todo.

Safety: write.

Requires a grant.

name: sys_cpu
description:
Show CPU model, core count and current usage

Safety: read.

cores.description: per-core usage as a bar chart

name: sys_disk
description:
Show disk usage per mounted filesystem

Safety: read.

all.description: include pseudo, duplicate and zero-size filesystems

name: sys_host
description:
Show host info: OS, kernel, uptime, addresses

Safety: read.

name: sys_load
description:
Show load averages, normalized per core

Safety: read.

name: sys_mem
description:
Show memory and swap usage

Safety: read.

name: sys_overview
description:
One-screen host health: cpu, memory, load, disk, uptime

A verdict and one line per subsystem, worst first: `status` (ok, or the worst fact), the fullest filesystem, memory by the kernel's pressure level (used memory where it publishes none), load per core, cpu, swap, then the host's name and uptime. A line that cannot be read says so, and so does the status. `numbers` carries the figures. `detail` expands into identity, per-core usage, memory and swap, every filesystem, sensors and top processes.

Safety: read.

name: sys_ps
description:
List top processes by CPU or memory

Ranks the processes this account can read, by CPU over a 200ms window or by memory. Another user's processes cannot be read without privileges, and one that ends during the scan is gone before it is, so both are left out and counted in a note under the table.

Also called: process, pid, hog, task, running.

Safety: read.

name: sys_temp
description:
Show sensor temperatures

Also called: temperature, thermal, hot, heat, celsius, overheating, fan.

Safety: read.

name: time_at
description:
Convert an instant between epoch, UTC, local time and a named zone

`when` takes an epoch number at any precision, an RFC3339 stamp, a plain date, or a duration either side of now (`90m ago`, `in 2h`); a bare number's unit is chosen by magnitude and stated in the `read-as` row. `zone` adds an IANA timezone. Rows are utc, local and epoch for now; `detail` adds `relative` and `epoch-ms`, always given for a named instant. A local time the clock showed twice is answered as one, the other in `ambiguous`; one it never showed is refused.

Also called: now, date, clock.

Safety: read.

when.description: an instant: now, an epoch number, 2026-09-04T12:00:00Z, 2026-09-04, or a relative duration like "90m ago"

zone.description: also show it in this IANA timezone (Europe/Paris)
